title: A nested Billing record on PlaceOrder carries @NotBlank constraints that no @Valid leads into
summary: Orders gain billing details for the receipt: a nested `Billing` record with `@NotBlank` and `@Email` on its fields, added to `PlaceOrder` as a `@NotNull` component. The handler validates the request with `@Valid`, so the author expects a blank name or a bad email to be refused. Bean Validation does not step into a nested object unless the property itself carries `@Valid`, so the only check that runs on the billing details is that they are present; every test posts valid ones and passes. The module's boundary contract lists each wire type with its constraints, and the regenerated contract has a `!` line under the new property saying that the constraints on `Billing` are not checked.

change.description: Collect the customer's billing name and email with the order, for the receipt. A nested `Billing` record is added to `OrderController` with `@NotBlank String name` and `@NotBlank @Email String email`, and `PlaceOrder` gains a `@NotNull Billing billing` component. The handler already takes the request as `@Valid @RequestBody PlaceOrder`. The order service does not use the details yet; that is the next change.

risk: `@Valid` on the handler parameter validates `PlaceOrder`'s own properties: `holdId`, `paymentToken` and now that `billing` is not null. Cascading into `billing` needs a `@Valid` on the component (or on the type argument, for a list); without it the validator never looks at `Billing`, and `{"name": "", "email": "not an address"}` is accepted. The constraints compile, the handler is annotated, the request type is annotated, and every test that posts an order sends a valid billing block, so nothing fails. The same shape covers a list of items (`List<Item>` where `Item` carries constraints) and a record extracted from a flat request during a refactor, which moves the constraints one level down and out of reach.
explanation: The wire block of the boundary contract lists each property of a request type with its constraints (`holdId: @NotBlank String`), as before. Under a property whose type carries constraints that no `@Valid` on the property or inside its type leads into, the contract has a `!` line. The change is intended, so the runner regenerates the contract and the reviewer reads the diff: a new `Billing` block with its two constrained properties, and under `PlaceOrder` the new line `billing: @NotNull Billing` followed by `! constraints on Billing are not checked: no @Valid on billing`. A new `!` line in the regenerated contract is the violation.
resolution: Write `@NotNull @Valid Billing billing`. The regenerated contract then shows `billing: @NotNull @Valid Billing` with no `!` line, which is the diff a reviewer approves. For a list, `List<@Valid Item>` or `@Valid List<Item>` both cascade, and the contract writes the type-use form into the type (`items: List<@Valid Item>`).
notes: The first example of the validation checks on a boundary contract (`lib/src/validation.rs`): a nested type's constraints with no `@Valid` leading into them (this example), a `@RequestBody` taken without `@Valid` or `@Validated` while its type carries constraints, a `@Valid` or `@Validated(G.class)` that leaves out the constraints of other groups, a constraint on a type its validator cannot handle (`@Size` on an `int`, which Hibernate Validator rejects at the first validation with `UnexpectedTypeException`), a null check on a primitive, and constraints on a non-public method of a `@Validated` bean. Each is a `!` line under the property or the handler; the library's Spring fixtures (`lib/tests/fixtures/spring/fixtures/spring/Booking.java`) have one of each.

The contract now writes the constraints inside a type, read from the class file's type annotations (`RuntimeVisibleTypeAnnotations`): `rows: @NotEmpty List<@Pattern(regexp = "[A-Z]") String>` in the ticketing service's `CreateConcert`, which earlier contracts showed as `List<String>`. The type-use constraints are where `List<@Valid Item>` cascades from, so a cascade check needs them.

The patch changes the Java of the module, so the runner compiles it with Gradle, reads the runtime class path through the build's `printRuntimeClasspath` task, and runs `jvmcontract update` then `verify` with `--resources` and `--classpath`. The Spring Boot tests of the module need Docker for Testcontainers; without it they fail before the change is tested, which the page records as the tests' result, not the verifier's.

The observation specs (`jvmcontract observations --against`, foundations O2), Box Office with this change against Box Office as it is (`lib/tests/observations.rs`, `box_office_examples_compare_as_their_boundary_diffs_say`): `POST /orders` gets two changed obligations. `inputs`: the body's wire shape gains `Billing` and `PlaceOrder: billing: @NotNull Billing`, with `PlaceOrder: billing: ! constraints on Billing are not checked: no @Valid on billing`, since the input domain is the preservation contract's. `status`: `MethodArgumentNotValidException` is now also for a body that fails `@NotNull on PlaceOrder.billing`, so a request the old build took is answered 400. That is the change of meaning a person approves. The unchecked `Billing` constraints are new behaviour with no old counterpart, so the comparison names them and doesn't count them as a regression.
provenance: Constructed from a validation gap that Spring Boot developers hit when a flat request grows a nested object: Bean Validation cascades only through @Valid, the handler's own @Valid looks one level deep, and tests that send valid data cannot tell.
